newsitem.title: UK: Cystic fibrosis tests could save costs - UK study.
newsitem.headline: Cystic fibrosis tests could save costs - UK study.

text.p: Screening newborn babies for cystic fibrosis could save tens of thousands of pounds (dollars) by allowing them to get early treatment, a British researcher said on Friday.

Treating a newborn baby helps prevent the lung damage that builds up during the repeated infections the disease can cause, Dr Jim Littlewood, chairman of the Cystic Fibrosis Trust's research medical advisory committee.
In a report timed to coincide with Cystic Fibrosis Week, he said the cost of treating a healthy newborn was about 10 percent that of treating a severely affected child.
"Babies, if they are not diagnosed early, will get damage to the chest from infection which you can never completely recover from," he said.
"The cost of treating a badly affected patient who requires a lot of antibiotics and nutritional support is 34,000 pounds ($55,000) a year. It is 4,000 pounds a year for a healthier patient."

Cystic fibrosis (CF) is the most common fatal recessive genetic disease among people of European origin. Among other things, it causes the lungs to overproduce mucus, which causes infection and scarring.
It is a favourite target of scientists developing gene therapy but they say the experimental treatment will do little good to patients with damaged organs.

Littlewood said a simple CF test would cost only 1.50 pounds. He said Italy, the Netherlands, Australia, France and the U.S. states of Wisconsin and Colorado already did such screening and had found it cost-effective.
Only about 20 percent of babies born in Britain are screened.
